catalog_quote: Ngunga 1997:16-17: 'This study is limited to segmental phonology. However, since Ciyao is a tonal language we will provide some brief notes on Ciyao tone without getting into a detailed description of its tonal system. Although Ciyao is said to have five phonetic tones, namely, high (H), low (L), downstep (!H), rising (LH) and falling (HL) (Whiteley 1966:7), phonemically there just two: H(igh) and L(ow) (Hyman and Ngunga 1994, Meeussen 1971, Mtenje 1990, Mtenje and Odden 1993, Odden 1994, 1997, Whiteley 1966) ... There is no lexical tonal contrast on verb roots. In Ciyao, verb tone is assigned by the inflectional morphology (tense/aspect system). ... Unlike verb roots, in which there is no H and L contrast, in nouns there is H and L contrast.' sweep_summary: One works with stress in the title (Philippson 1991, the 542-page Paris V thesis on tone and accent in East Bantu). theses.fr marks it not accessible and it is absent from HAL, archive.org and Persée, but an open full-text PDF (text layer, 542 pp.) is linked from the author's DDL/CNRS CV page and was downloaded, saved and read: Yao (P21) is one of the ~20 '++' core languages, gets its own case study (ch.4 sec.2.4, pp.102-109), is typed '(a):7, (b):1' (7 noun-stem tone patterns, no verb-stem contrast, Tableau II p.78), is called 'une langue très tonale' (p.251), is placed at diachronic 'stade I' (tonal assimilation without neutralisation, p.487), and in the annex fiche (pp.506-507) is coded 'langue tonale' with the penultimate's status given only as a tone-realisation rule; p.483 states outright that the penultimate plays no important role in the purely tonal systems, 'faible en yao'. This CONFIRMS the catalog's 'tonal' coding and supplies the explicit modern negative on penultimate accent that the catalog's deciding source (Ngunga 1997, silent on stress) lacked; recommend adding Philippson 1991 pp.78, 483-484, 506-507 as a supporting citation (does not replace Ngunga 1997). A related 1998 Faits de Langues summary article (doi:10.3406/flang.1998.1225) was surfaced by Crossref but is behind Persée's altcha challenge; low priority since the thesis itself was read.fr, HAL, Crossref, archive.org and the DDL site.

new_statements.translation: [Annex, rubrics:] 3. tonal or accentual system ... 10. status of the penultimate syllable. — Yao: 1.: yes [surface vowel-length contrast] / 3.: tone language / 4.: 3 [tone patterns on] -CVCV [noun stems], 5 [on] -CV:CV / 6.: [Meeussen's rule] present / 7.: systematic (post-lexical) / 10.: LL.H• is realised LH.L. — In general, apart from these last two languages [Chaga, Kamba], the penultimate does not seem to play an important role in the purely tonal systems (none in Nyamwezi, Bemba and Kikuyu, weak in Yao and Sukuma).

new_statements.reading: A first-hand comparatist who lists Yao among his best-described core languages classifies Yao as a tone language (lexical tone contrast on nouns, none on verb stems; all four Common-Bantu patterns retained; Meeussen's rule post-lexical) and explicitly rates the penultimate's role as weak, limited to one tone-realisation rule — i.e. no demarcative penultimate accent and no word-stress rule. This is the only modern source found that addresses the stress/accent axis for Yao head-on rather than being silent on it; it confirms the catalog's 'tonal' coding and closes the gap B flagged (modern sources silent rather than negative on stress).

audit.reasoning: (1) Both deciding quotations are present verbatim in the copies we hold at the stated sections; only nit is that the Ngunga passage sits on printed pp.17-18 rather than '16-17'. (2) The tonal coding rests on a 1997 Berkeley dissertation by the language's principal native-speaker phonologist, which states outright that Ciyao is tonal (H vs L, morphological verb tone) and never posits stress; Odden 2003 (held, read now) says the same for all of zone P and attributes penultimate lengthening to Makonde, not Yao; Hyman & Ngunga 1997 (downloaded now, open) is likewise stress-free. (3) The pre-tonal missionary record, now complete held by the project, is internally split but reconcilable with the tonal reading: Steere 1871 hears near-even accent with the penult 'a little louder', Hetherwick 1889/1902 'usually penultimate, more rarely antepenult, never final', Sanderson 1922 'impossible to frame any rule.. never

sources.note: Yao is treated throughout as a tone language, never as an accent language: 7 distinct tone patterns on disyllabic noun stems and a single (non-contrastive) pattern on verb stems (Tableau II p.78); 'une langue très tonale' whose verb-root equivalents carry no tonal opposition (p.251); one of the few East Bantu languages that preserved all four Common-Bantu patterns BB/BH/HB/HH, though tones are not realised directly on the syllables that bear them (p.460, p.478); Meeussen's rule present but post-lexical (pp.106-109, 469, 478); diachronic 'stade I' = tonal assimilation without neutralisation (p…

sources.citation: Hetherwick, Alexander. 1902. A handbook of the Yao language. London: SPCK (archive.org ahandbookyaolan00hethgoog).
sources.access_detail: a copy the project holds (available on request)
sources.quote: 'In Yao the accent usually falls on the penultimate syllable (majzeimba), more rarely on the antepenult (wangali, waichile), never on the final syllable. When a suffix is appended to a word, the accent sometimes shifts so as to be on the penult (kumpilikina, kumpilikanila); sometimes it remains on its original syllable (waiche, waichile). The addition of the enclitic syllables -je, -ga, always draws forward the accent.'
